claims.text: Conventionally processed W–Cu composites have a randomly distributed two-phase microstructure.
Tungsten forms a mechanically robust framework in the baseline W–Cu composite.
The tungsten framework is irradiation resistant.
Copper provides the high-thermal-conductivity phase in the W–Cu composite.
Directional solidification can produce continuous, aligned copper channels embedded in a tungsten matrix.
Controlled cooling rates promote alignment of the copper phase during fabrication.
Continuous copper channels provide efficient pathways for electron transport.
Continuous copper channels provide efficient pathways for phonon transport.
Aligning the copper channels reduces heat-carrier scattering associated with randomly oriented phase boundaries.
Reduced heat-carrier scattering increases the composite's net thermal conductivity.
The tungsten matrix remains the primary load-bearing phase after directional solidification.
Retention of the tungsten matrix preserves the composite's mechanical durability.
Retention of the tungsten matrix preserves the composite's irradiation tolerance.
The directionally solidified W–Cu composite will have significantly higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable randomly structured W–Cu composite.
The thermal-conductivity increase could be approximately 20% relative to the baseline.
The directionally solidified composite will maintain mechanical strength similar to that of the baseline composite.
The directionally solidified composite will maintain irradiation resistance similar to that of the baseline composite.
The predicted benefit applies over elevated operating temperatures relevant to heat-dissipation systems and fusion-reactor joints.
The predicted benefit applies under fusion-relevant irradiation environments.
The benefit depends on the aligned copper network remaining continuous and stable without coarsening or phase instability during prolonged high-temperature or irradiation exposure.
